claim: Zippering of SNARE complexes spanning docked membranes is essential for most intracellular fusion events.
source: Zippering of SNARE complexes spanning docked membranes is essential for most intracellular fusion events.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established scientific knowledge about SNARE-mediated fusion.

claim: HOPS and its SM subunit Vps33 catalyze the formation of a metastable trans-complex.
source: The formation of a metastable trans-complex, catalyzed by HOPS and its SM subunit Vps33, is followed by subsequent zippering transitions that increase the probability of fusion.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sec17 (α-SNAP) can either inhibit or stimulate SNARE-mediated fusion, operating independently of Sec18 (NSF) catalysis.
source: Operating independently of Sec18 (NSF) catalysis, Sec17 (α-SNAP) either inhibits or stimulates SNARE-mediated fusion.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 3-6 and 10.

claim: If HOPS or Vps33 are absent, Sec17 inhibits fusion at an early stage.
source: If HOPS or Vps33 are absent, Sec17 inhibits fusion at an early stage.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 10.

claim: Vps33/HOPS promotes productive SNARE assembly in the presence of otherwise inhibitory Sec17.
source: Thus, Vps33/HOPS promotes productive SNARE assembly in the presence of otherwise inhibitory Sec17.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 7 and 10.

claim: Once SNAREs are partially zipped, Sec17 promotes fusion in either the presence or absence of HOPS.
source: Once SNAREs are partially zipped, Sec17 promotes fusion in either the presence or absence of HOPS, but with faster kinetics when HOPS is absent, suggesting that ejection of the SM is a rate-limiting step.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 10D.

claim: Sec17 promotes fusion with faster kinetics when HOPS is absent compared to when HOPS is present.
source: Once SNAREs are partially zipped, Sec17 promotes fusion in either the presence or absence of HOPS, but with faster kinetics when HOPS is absent, suggesting that ejection of the SM is a rate-limiting step.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by kinetic data in Figure 10D.

claim: Ejection of the SM is a rate-limiting step in SNARE-mediated fusion.
source: Once SNAREs are partially zipped, Sec17 promotes fusion in either the presence or absence of HOPS, but with faster kinetics when HOPS is absent, suggesting that ejection of the SM is a rate-limiting step.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that fusion is faster without HOPS.

claim: SNAREs confer inherent compartmental selectivity.
source: SNAREs confer inherent compartmental selectivity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work (Izawa et al., 2012; McNew et al., 2000).

claim: Only a subset of possible SNARE complex permutations assemble into kinetically stable complexes.
source: Among the many possible permutations of SNARE complexes, only a subset assemble into kinetically stable complexes; among these, only a further subset efficiently initiate fusion (Izawa et al., 2012; McNew et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Among kinetically stable SNARE complexes, only a subset efficiently initiate fusion.
source: Among the many possible permutations of SNARE complexes, only a subset assemble into kinetically stable complexes; among these, only a further subset efficiently initiate fusion (Izawa et al., 2012; McNew et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The folded portion of a SNARE complex is a parallel bundle of four α-helical SNARE domains (Qa, Qb, Qc, and R).
source: The folded portion of a SNARE complex is a parallel bundle of four α-helical SNARE domains (Qa, Qb, Qc, and R; Fasshauer et al., 1998; Hanson et al., 1997; Poirier et al., 1998; Sutton et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: N-to-C zippering of the trans-SNARE complex generates mechanical tension.
source: N-to-C zippering of the trans-SNARE complex generates mechanical tension (Hanson et al., 1997; Liu et al., 2006; Min et al., 2013; Zorman et al., 2014), driving the SNARE C-termini and their associated membranes together to initiate lipid mixing and fusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: SNARE zippering drives the SNARE C-termini and their associated membranes together to initiate lipid mixing and fusion.
source: N-to-C zippering of the trans-SNARE complex generates mechanical tension (Hanson et al., 1997; Liu et al., 2006; Min et al., 2013; Zorman et al., 2014), driving the SNARE C-termini and their associated membranes together to initiate lipid mixing and fusion.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description supported by citations.

claim: After fusion, SNARE complex membrane anchors lie in cis, adjacent and parallel within the membrane.
source: After fusion, the SNARE complex membrane anchors lie in cis, adjacent and parallel within the membrane.
evidence: This describes the post-fusion state of SNARE complexes, which is established knowledge.

claim: Cis-SNARE complexes are disassembled to recycle and energize the SNAREs for subsequent fusion reactions.
source: Cis-complexes are then disassembled to recycle and energize the SNAREs for subsequent fusion reactions (Hanson et al., 1997; Mayer et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Disassembly of cis-SNARE complexes requires the Sec18 ATPase and Sec17.
source: Disassembly requires the Sec18 ATPase and Sec17, an adapter that docks Sec18 onto the SNARE complex (Hanson et al., 1997; Mayer et al., 1996; Söllner et al., 1993; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sec17 is an adapter that docks Sec18 onto the SNARE complex.
source: Disassembly requires the Sec18 ATPase and Sec17, an adapter that docks Sec18 onto the SNARE complex (Hanson et al., 1997; Mayer et al., 1996; Söllner et al., 1993; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This functional description is supported by citations.

claim: In mammals, Sec18 and Sec17 are named NSF and α-SNAP.
source: In mammals, Sec18 and Sec17 are named NSF and α-SNAP.
evidence: This is a nomenclature statement that is established knowledge.

claim: All SNARE-mediated fusion events that have been closely examined require cofactors of the Sec1/Mammalian UNC-18 (SM) family.
source: Diverse factors operate at specific compartments, but all SNARE-mediated fusion events that have been closely examined require cofactors of the Sec1/Mammalian UNC-18 (SM) family (Baker and Hughson, 2016; Carr and Rizo, 2010; Südhof and Rothman, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple review citations.

claim: In vitro, SM proteins increase the rate of fusion several-fold above the basal rate catalyzed by SNAREs alone.
source: In vitro, SM proteins increase the rate of fusion several-fold above the basal rate catalyzed by SNAREs alone (Furukawa and Mima, 2014; Shen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: In vivo, SM deletion annihilates fusion.
source: In vivo, however, SM deletion annihilates fusion (Carr and Rizo, 2010; Südhof and Rothman, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to in vivo studies.

claim: The HOPS tethering complex controls endolysosomal docking and fusion.
source: Here, we examine SM function in the context of the HOPS tethering complex, which controls endolysosomal docking and fusion (Rieder and Emr, 1997; Seals et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The HOPS SM subunit Vps33 is both necessary and sufficient for HOPS interaction with SNARE domains and SNARE complexes.
source: Importantly, the HOPS SM subunit Vps33 is both necessary and sufficient for HOPS interaction with SNARE domains and SNARE complexes (Dulubova et al., 2001; Krämer and Ungermann, 2011; Lobingier et al., 2014; Lobingier and Merz, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including authors' previous work.

claim: Crystal structures reveal how the Qa- and R-SNARE interact with Vps33 in a pre-fusion state.
source: A pair of breakthrough crystal structures seems to reveal how the Qa- and R-SNARE interact with Vps33 in a pre-fusion state (Baker et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to structural work.

claim: Vps33 nucleates and guides assembly of the partially zipped trans-SNARE complex.
source: These structures strongly support the hypothesis that Vps33 nucleates and guides assembly of the partially zipped trans-SNARE complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of structural data cited in the previous sentence.

claim: The mechanism by which Vps33 nucleates trans-SNARE assembly may be common to all SMs.
source: The same mechanism may be common to all SMs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generality of the mechanism.

claim: Sec17 interacts with both post-fusion and pre-fusion SNARE complexes.
source: The disassembly adapter Sec17 interacts not only with post-fusion SNARE complexes, but also with pre-fusion SNARE complexes as well (Barszczewski et al., 2008; Park et al., 2014; Schwartz and Merz, 2009; Song et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2000; Xu et al., 2010; Zick et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including authors' previous work.

claim: Sec17 has been reported to both inhibit and stimulate fusion.
source: In an apparent paradox, Sec17 has been reported to both inhibit and stimulate fusion.
evidence: This statement summarizes conflicting findings from the literature.

claim: The fusion-augmenting activity of Sec17 was first observed in cell-free assays with intact native yeast vacuoles bearing stalled, partially zipped SNARE complexes.
source: The fusion-augmenting activity of Sec17 was first observed in cell-free assays with intact native yeast vacuoles bearing stalled, partially zipped SNARE complexes (Schwartz and Merz, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Binding of Sec17 to trans-SNARE complexes stabilizes the folded state of the trans-SNARE complex's membrane-proximal C-terminal domain.
source: To explain these unexpected results, we proposed that binding of Sec17 to trans-SNARE complexes stabilizes the folded state of the trans-SNARE complex's membrane-proximal C-terminal domain (Schwartz and Merz, 2009).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed by the authors in previous work.

claim: Single-molecule force spectroscopy experiments provided direct evidence for the zipper-clamp mechanism.
source: More recently, single-molecule force spectroscopy experiments provided direct evidence for this zipper-clamp mechanism (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to force spectroscopy work.

claim: Sec18, either with or without ATP hydrolysis, enhances the Sec17 stimulation of fusion.
source: Experiments with proteoliposomes demonstrated that Sec18, either with or without ATP hydrolysis, further enhances the Sec17 stimulation of fusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results from proteoliposome studies.

claim: Membrane penetration by a hydrophobic loop near the Sec17 N-terminus may contribute to Sec17's fusogenic activity.
source: Moreover, membrane penetration by a hydrophobic loop near the Sec17 N-terminus may contribute to Sec17's fusogenic activity (Song et al., 2017; Zick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: SM activity becomes essential in the presence of molecular crowding agents.
source: In reconstitution experiments, SM activity becomes essential in the presence of molecular crowding agents (Furukawa and Mima, 2014; Yu et al., 2015) or in the presence of Sec17 and Sec18 (Ma et al., 2013; Mima et al., 2008; Starai et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reconstitution studies.

claim: SM activity becomes essential in the presence of Sec17 and Sec18.
source: In reconstitution experiments, SM activity becomes essential in the presence of molecular crowding agents (Furukawa and Mima, 2014; Yu et al., 2015) or in the presence of Sec17 and Sec18 (Ma et al., 2013; Mima et al., 2008; Starai et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reconstitution studies.

claim: Sec17 and SMs can physically associate with one another on quaternary SNARE complexes.
source: Sec17 and SMs can physically associate with one another on quaternary SNARE complexes, and SNARE-bound Golgi or vacuole SM proteins directly impede Sec18-mediated SNARE disassembly (Lobingier et al., 2014), conferring resistance to Sec18-mediated trans-complex disassembly (He et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations including authors' previous work.

claim: SNARE-bound SM proteins directly impede Sec18-mediated SNARE disassembly.
source: Sec17 and SMs can physically associate with one another on quaternary SNARE complexes, and SNARE-bound Golgi or vacuole SM proteins directly impede Sec18-mediated SNARE disassembly (Lobingier et al., 2014), conferring resistance to Sec18-mediated trans-complex disassembly (He et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: SM proteins confer resistance to Sec18-mediated trans-complex disassembly.
source: Sec17 and SMs can physically associate with one another on quaternary SNARE complexes, and SNARE-bound Golgi or vacuole SM proteins directly impede Sec18-mediated SNARE disassembly (Lobingier et al., 2014), conferring resistance to Sec18-mediated trans-complex disassembly (He et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Qc-wt or Qc-7∆ knock-in cells had morphologically normal vacuoles.
source: Consistent with previous in vitro experiments (Schwartz and Merz, 2009), Qc-wt or Qc-7∆ knock-in cells had morphologically normal vacuoles (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Qc-1∆, Qc-3∆, Qc-5∆ knock-in cells had fragmented vacuoles and were phenotypically indistinguishable from the vam7∆ null mutant.
source: while Qc-1∆, Qc-3∆, Qc-5∆ knock-in cells had fragmented vacuoles and were phenotypically indistinguishable from the vam7∆ null mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Overproduction of Qc-1∆, −3∆, or −5∆ proteins in vam7∆ cells resulted in complete vacuolar fragmentation.
source: Overproduction of Qc-1∆, −3∆, or −5∆ proteins in vam7∆ cells (which lack Qc-wt) also resulted in complete vacuolar fragmentation (Figure 2B, top row).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Qc-3∆ and Qc-5∆ nucleate stalled trans-SNARE complexes, while Qc-1∆ does not enter stable trans-SNARE complexes.
source: Previously, we reported that in vitro, Qc-3∆ and Qc-5∆ nucleate stalled trans-SNARE complexes, while Qc-1∆ does not enter stable trans-SNARE complexes (Schwartz and Merz, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: In wild-type VAM7 cells, overproduction of Qc-3∆ or Qc-5∆, but not Qc-1∆, caused dominant fragmentation of the vacuole with 30–40% penetrance.
source: Consistent with the in vitro experiments, in wild-type VAM7 cells overproduction of Qc-3∆ or Qc-5∆, but not Qc-1∆, caused dominant fragmentation of the vacuole with 30–40% penetrance (Figure 2B, bottom row).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cells expressing Qc-1∆, −3∆, or −5∆ as knock-ins at the chromosomal VAM7 locus had ALP and CPY maturation defects as severe as the vam7∆ null mutant.
source: Cells expressing Qc-1∆, −3∆, or −5∆ as knock-ins at the chromosomal VAM7 locus had ALP and CPY maturation defects as severe as the vam7∆ null mutant (Figure 2C, compare lane 2 to lanes 5–7).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In VAM7 wild-type cells, Qc-3∆ or Qc-5∆ overproduction caused dominant, partial defects in ALP maturation.
source: In VAM7 wild-type cells, Qc-3∆ or Qc-5∆ overproduction caused dominant, partial defects in ALP maturation (Figure 2D, lanes 18 and 19).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In wild-type cells overproducing Qc-5∆, the median number of AP-3 vesicles nearly doubled.
source: In wild-type cells overproducing Qc-5∆, the median number of AP-3 vesicles nearly doubled (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: In Qc-5∆-overproducer cells, AP-3 puncta were observed in clumps at the vacuole-limiting membrane.
source: Moreover, in Qc-5∆-overproducer cells, AP-3 puncta were observed in clumps at the vacuole-limiting membrane (Figure 2E, arrow), rather than dispersed throughout the cytoplasm as in vam7∆ cells (lacking the vacuolar Qc).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The AP-3 vesicle coat does not dissociate until after zippering of the SNARE C-terminal domain, and perhaps following fusion.
source: This suggests a defect in fusion but not docking. Moreover, it further suggests that the AP-3 vesicle coat does not dissociate until after zippering of the SNARE C-terminal domain, and perhaps following fusion (Angers and Merz, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization of AP-3 vesicles, supported by a citation.

claim: Qc-2∆ and Qc-4∆ did not drive fusion, even when added at high concentrations.
source: Unlike Qc-wt, neither Qc-2∆ nor Qc-4∆ drove fusion, even when added at high concentrations (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Qc-2∆, like Qc-1∆, was weakly inhibitory in competitive inhibition assays.
source: Here, added Qc-2∆, like Qc-1∆, was weakly inhibitory, while Qc-4∆, like Qc-3∆, was a potent competitive inhibitor (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive inhibition data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Qc-4∆, like Qc-3∆, was a potent competitive inhibitor of fusion.
source: Here, added Qc-2∆, like Qc-1∆, was weakly inhibitory, while Qc-4∆, like Qc-3∆, was a potent competitive inhibitor (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive inhibition data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Qc-4∆ enters into partially zipped but fusion-defective trans-SNARE complexes.
source: We infer that Qc-4∆, like Qc-3∆ (Schwartz and Merz, 2009; Xu et al., 2010), enters into partially zipped but fusion-defective trans-SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the competitive inhibition data and comparison to Qc-3∆.

claim: Sec17 addition restores the ability of Qc-3∆ to drive fusion in the absence of Sec18 or ATP.
source: Sec17 addition restores the ability of Qc-3∆ to drive fusion in the absence of Sec18 or ATP (Schwartz and Merz, 2009; Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: In no-ATP gain-of-function reactions containing added Sec17, Qc-4∆ drove fusion with a dose-response relationship indistinguishable from that of Qc-3∆.
source: In no-ATP gain-of-function reactions containing added Sec17, Qc-4∆ drove fusion with a dose-response relationship indistinguishable from that of Qc-3∆ (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Sec17 failed to rescue fusion in reactions containing Qc-2∆.
source: In marked contrast, Sec17 failed to rescue fusion in reactions containing Qc-2∆ (see Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The propensity to form a metastable trans complex increases in a switch-like manner as the Qc-SNARE is extended from layer +2 to layer +3 or +4.
source: Taken together, these results and previous work (Schwartz and Merz, 2009) indicate that the propensity to form a metastable trans complex increases in a switch-like manner as the Qc-SNARE is extended from layer +2 to layer +3 or +4.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from Figures 3A-C and previous work.

claim: In a 'half-zipped' state the neuronal R-SNARE is structured to approximately layer +2, and the t/Q-SNARE complex is structured to layer +4.
source: Force spectroscopy studies show that in a 'half-zipped' state the neuronal R-SNARE is structured to approximately layer +2, and the t/Q-SNARE complex is structured to layer +4 (Ma et al., 2015; Min et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016; Zorman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to force spectroscopy studies.

claim: With a stalled trans-complex zipped to Qc layer +3 or +4, the docked membranes should be separated by 8–10 nm, fully hydrated and unable to initiate lipid mixing.
source: With a stalled trans-complex zipped to Qc layer +3 or +4, the docked membranes should be separated by 8–10 nm, fully hydrated and unable to initiate lipid mixing.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural considerations and force spectroscopy data.

claim: The propensity of the partially zipped trans-complex to initiate fusion increases abruptly when Sec17 is added or by extending Qc-4∆ a single α-helical turn, from +4 to +5.
source: The propensity of the partially zipped trans-complex to initiate fusion increases abruptly, either when Sec17 is added or by extending Qc-4∆ a single α-helical turn, from +4 to+5 (Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figures 3C and 3E.

claim: Fusion is maximal when the Qc is extended to layer +7.
source: Fusion is maximal when the Qc is extended to layer +7 (Schwartz and Merz, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: A transition barrier between the partially zipped state and C-terminal domain trans-complex zippering is traversed as R-SNARE assembly proceeds through layer +3, +4, or +5.
source: Our results again are consistent with force spectroscopy experiments, where a transition barrier between the partially zipped state and C-terminal domain trans-complex zippering is traversed as R-SNARE assembly proceeds through layer +3,+4, or +5, depending on the specific complex (Min et al., 2013; Zorman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to force spectroscopy studies and is consistent with the authors' data.

claim: Mutation of the non-conserved first Arg to Ala (AR) in Qc-5∆ slightly increased fusion versus 'wild-type' (RR) Qc-5∆.
source: In gain-of-function 'bypass' reactions lacking ATP (Figure 3E), mutation of the non-conserved first Arg to Ala (AR) slightly increased fusion versus 'wild-type'(RR) Qc-5∆.
evidence: This claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mutation of the second, conserved Arg (RA) in Qc-5∆ decreased fusion.
source: Mutation of the second, conserved Arg (RA) decreased fusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mutation of both arginyl residues (AA) in Qc-5∆ further impaired fusion.
source: Mutation of both residues (AA) further impaired fusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The apparent KM (EC50) values for the mutant Qc-5∆s (AR, RA, AA) were indistinguishable from 'wild-type' Qc-5∆ (RR).
source: In both assay configurations, the apparent KM (EC50) values for the mutant Qc-5∆s (AR, RA, AA) were indistinguishable from 'wild-type' Qc-5∆ (RR).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of dose-response data in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: The ability of Qc-5∆ mutants to assemble into pre-fusion complexes was unaltered, even as their capacity to drive fusion diverged.
source: Thus, the ability of these Qc-5∆ mutants to assemble into pre-fusion complexes was unaltered, even as their capacity to drive fusion diverged.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EC50 data from Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Added Sec17 allowed all Qc-5∆ variants to drive fusion with similar efficiency.
source: Moreover, added Sec17 allowed all Qc-5∆ variants to drive fusion with similar efficiency (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Qc layer +5 has a pivotal role in fusion, probably driving C-terminal zippering beyond the 'half-zipped' metastable state and through the transition barrier.
source: These findings, and results from other systems (Fasshauer et al., 1998; Mohrmann et al., 2010; Sakaba et al., 2005) indicate that Qc layer +5 has a pivotal role in fusion, probably driving C-terminal zippering beyond the 'half-zipped' metastable state and through the transition barrier separating partially zipped and C-terminally zipped trans-complexes (Liu et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2016; Min et al., 2013; Zorman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by multiple citations.

claim: The transition between the partially zipped and C-terminally zipped states likely results in ejection of the bound SM cofactor Vps33.
source: As discussed below, the transition between the partially zipped and C-terminally zipped states likely also results in ejection of the bound SM cofactor Vps33.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis that will be discussed later in the manuscript.

claim: Sec17 (α-SNAP)-binding promotes zippering of the SNARE bundle's C-terminal domain.
source: Our results with intact vacuoles also mirror force spectroscopy studies done in solution, which show that Sec17 (α-SNAP)-binding promotes zippering of the SNARE bundle's C-terminal domain (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to force spectroscopy work.

claim: In reactions lacking Sec18, when HOPS and full-length Qc-wt were added to RPLs, fusion was rapid and efficient whether Sec17 was added to the reaction or not.
source: In reactions lacking Sec18, when HOPS and full-length Qc-wt were added to RPLs, fusion was rapid and efficient whether Sec17 was added to the reaction or not (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RPL fusion assay data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The truncation mutants Qc-3∆, −4∆, and −5∆ were non-fusogenic unless Sec17 was supplied.
source: In contrast to Qc-wt, the truncation mutants Qc-3∆, −4∆, and −5∆ were non-fusogenic unless Sec17 was supplied (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RPL fusion assay data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: In the absence of Sec17, Sec18 was unable to rescue Qc truncation mutants.
source: In the absence of Sec17, Sec18 was unable to rescue Qc truncation mutants (Figure 4A,D,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RPL fusion assay data shown in Figure 4A,D,G.

claim: Sec18 dramatically enhanced Sec17-mediated rescue and allowed fusion with the Qc-∆ proteins, at much lower Sec17 concentrations.
source: However, Sec18 dramatically enhanced Sec17-mediated rescue and allowed fusion with the Qc-∆ proteins, at much lower Sec17 concentrations (Figure 4D–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by RPL fusion assay data shown in Figure 4D-I.

claim: Qc-5∆ always had more fusion activity than Qc-3∆ or Qc-4∆.
source: Qc-5∆ always had more fusion activity than Qc-3∆ or Qc-4∆, underscoring the interplay between Sec17 stimulation and trans-SNARE zippering.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of fusion activities across Figure 4 panels.

claim: Sec17 rescue of partially zipped SNARE complexes can occur in the total absence of Sec18.
source: At this point, we can draw several conclusions. First, Sec17 rescue of partially zipped SNARE complexes can occur in the total absence of Sec18.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the RPL data in Figure 4.

claim: Rigor-locked Sec18-ATP can augment the Sec17 rescue of Qc-3∆ without any requirement for ATP hydrolysis.
source: In parallel work, we demonstrated that rigor-locked Sec18-ATP can augment the Sec17 rescue of Qc-3∆ without any requirement for ATP hydrolysis (Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to parallel work by the authors.

claim: When present, Sec18 need not disassemble SNARE complexes to facilitate Sec17-mediated triggering of fusion.
source: Thus, when present, Sec18 need not disassemble SNARE complexes to facilitate Sec17-mediated triggering of fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and the parallel work cited.

claim: Sec17 supports Qc-∆–mediated fusion in the total absence of full-length Qc-wt.
source: Second, full-length Vam7 (Qc-wt) might be available in residual quantities on intact vacuoles, but it is not present in the chemically defined Qc-∆ RPL reactions. Thus, Sec17 supports Qc-∆–mediated fusion in the total absence of full-length Qc-wt.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RPL experimental design and results.

claim: No additional vacuolar proteins are needed for Sec17 stimulation of fusion.
source: Third, no additional vacuolar proteins are needed for Sec17 stimulation of fusion.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the chemically defined RPL system.

claim: Sec17 stimulation of fusion is observed both with native vacuole membranes and with RPLs, even at physiological or below-physiological SNARE, Rab, and HOPS concentrations.
source: Importantly, Sec17 stimulation of fusion is observed both with native vacuole membranes and with RPLs, even at physiological or below-physiological SNARE, Rab, and HOPS concentrations (Schwartz and Merz, 2009; Song et al., 2017; Zick et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies by the authors.

claim: Sec17/α-SNAP has been reported to inhibit fusion of yeast vacuoles and dense core secretory vesicles.
source: In addition to the canonical role of Sec17 in cis-SNARE complex disassembly, and its ability to augment the fusion capacity of SNARE complexes, Sec17/α-SNAP has also been reported to inhibit fusion of yeast vacuoles and dense core secretory vesicles (Park et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sec17 interacts with SNARE proteins through a large concave binding surface.
source: Sec17 interacts with SNARE proteins through a large concave binding surface, it interacts with Sec18 through its C-terminal domain, and it interacts with membranes through an N-terminal hydrophobic loop (Barnard et al., 1996; Hanson et al., 1997; Lauer et al., 2006; Marz et al., 2003; Schwartz and Merz, 2009; Winter et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing Sec17 structure and interactions.

claim: Sec17 interacts with Sec18 through its C-terminal domain.
source: Sec17 interacts with SNARE proteins through a large concave binding surface, it interacts with Sec18 through its C-terminal domain, and it interacts with membranes through an N-terminal hydrophobic loop (Barnard et al., 1996; Hanson et al., 1997; Lauer et al., 2006; Marz et al., 2003; Schwartz and Merz, 2009; Winter et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sec17 interacts with membranes through an N-terminal hydrophobic loop.
